title: The new moon
hook: each new month is a small holiday, long honored especially by women

segments.voice: Yesterday, the luach: a calendar of moon months, with a leap month to keep the seasons. Your line was the moon keeps time. Did you catch the sunset, the moment a new day began? Day one hundred twenty-two.

A hilltop near Jerusalem, just after sunset, in the days the Mishnah describes. Two people are squinting at the western sky, looking for the thinnest sliver of moon, barely there. They see it. They hurry to the court in Jerusalem and testify. The judges question them: where was it, which way did it point? When the testimony holds, the court declares it: the new month has begun. The Mishnah says that news once traveled by torches waved from mountaintop to mountaintop, all the way to the Jews in Babylon. All that, for the first day of a month.
screen: `A SLIVER OF MOON AT SUNSET.` → `WITNESSES RUN TO THE COURT.` → `TORCHES FROM HILL TO HILL.`

segments.voice: The first day of every Jewish month has a name: Rosh Chodesh. Rosh means head, and chodesh means month, from a root that means new. So the Hebrew month is named for the moon's renewal. Every month starts with a small holiday. It isn't a day off work. But in the synagogue there's an extra prayer service, the psalms of praise called Hallel are sung in a shorter form, and a special Torah reading is added. In the Torah itself, the new moons stand beside the festivals: the Book of Numbers speaks of blowing trumpets "in the day of your gladness, and in your appointed seasons, and in your new moons." In the Bible's stories, it's a day for a family meal; King Saul notices that David's seat is empty at the new moon feast. Rosh Chodesh also has a long tie to women. A midrash tells that when the people built the golden calf, the women refused to hand over their gold jewelry for it, and so they were given the new moons as a holiday of their own. Jewish law records a custom of women setting aside some work on the day. In recent decades, some Jewish women have gathered in Rosh Chodesh groups, to study, sing and talk, month by month. There's one more custom: a few days after the new moon, when the moon is growing, some Jews go outside at night and say a blessing over it. Why does the moon matter so much? Because it shrinks, disappears, and comes back. The blessing said over the moon makes the comparison itself: it speaks of the Jewish people as destined to be renewed like the moon.
screen: `ROSH CHODESH: HEAD OF THE MONTH.` · `A SMALL HOLIDAY EVERY MONTH.` · `A DAY FOR WOMEN.` · `THE MOON SHRINKS AND COMES BACK.` · then, large: `AND IN YOUR NEW MOONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for the moon tonight. Before that, settle, and breathe. Think about where the moon is right now, even if you can't see it: growing, full, shrinking, or gone dark. Then think of one part of your life that feels like the dark of the moon, something that's gone quiet. You don't have to fix it. Just remember that dark is part of the cycle, not the end of it. The bell holds the time.
Rosh Chodesh. The head of the month: the new moon, kept as a small holiday, and long honored as a day for women.
Your line: renew with the moon. Tonight, step outside and find the moon, or the place where it would be, and let one thing start over. Day one hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: On Rosh Chodesh, synagogues add a short Hallel, a Torah reading and an additional service. Some women mark the day with study groups or by setting aside some work, and some communities bless the growing moon a few days later.

original.note: Hebrew: head of the month. chodesh comes from chadash, new.

trapdoor: what you thought: just the first day of the month.
what it means: a small holiday every month, with extra prayers, long honored as a day for women.
what a scholar hears: chodesh shares a root with chadash, new; the midrash on the golden calf is in Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, and the torch signals are described in Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 2.

notes: Women and Rosh Chodesh: Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 45; the custom of women refraining from some work is cited in the Tur (Orach Chayim 417). Confirm citations.
Torch signals from mountaintops: Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 2:2–4; 'all the way to Babylon' (Golah) per 2:4. Confirm.
Kiddush Levanah (blessing the moon) described generically; timing customs differ (from 3 or 7 days after the molad).
Moon as a picture of Israel's renewal: drawn from the Kiddush Levanah liturgy and Sanhedrin 42a; stated loosely as 'the rabbis saw'.
